claim: The position of switch I differs appreciably between myosins, resulting in varying positions of the coordinated Mg2+ ion.

claim: While the general architecture of the active site is common to all myosins, small local reorganizations occur and possibly account for the different kinetics within the myosin superfamily.

claim: The overall structures of the strong-ADP states of myosin-V, -IB, and -XV differ considerably, resulting in lever arm orientations deviating by 71° and 22°, respectively.

evidence: This is supported by comparison with other structures.

claim: The structure of the actomyosin-V complex in the absence of any nucleotide in myosin represents the rigor state.

claim: The rigor state has an unoccupied and open active site.
source: In addition to an unoccupied and open active site (Figure 2—video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), the actin-binding cleft is closed, facilitating strong binding to F-actin, and the lever arm adopts a post-powerstroke orientation (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 1).

claim: In the rigor state, the actin-binding cleft is closed, facilitating strong binding to F-actin.
source: In addition to an unoccupied and open active site (Figure 2—video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), the actin-binding cleft is closed, facilitating strong binding to F-actin, and the lever arm adopts a post-powerstroke orientation (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: In the rigor state, the lever arm adopts a post-powerstroke orientation.
source: In addition to an unoccupied and open active site (Figure 2—video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), the actin-binding cleft is closed, facilitating strong binding to F-actin, and the lever arm adopts a post-powerstroke orientation (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: The features of the rigor state (unoccupied and open active site, closed actin-binding cleft, post-powerstroke lever arm orientation) are common to all rigor structures solved to date.
source: These features are common to all rigor structures solved to date (Banerjee et al., 2017; Behrmann et al., 2012; Doran et al., 2020; Fujii and Namba, 2017; Gong et al., 2021; Gurel et al., 2017; Mentes et al., 2018; Risi et al., 2021; Robert-Paganin et al., 2021; Vahokoski et al., 2020; von der Ecken et al., 2016).

claim: The structures of different myosins vary, particularly in the orientation of the lever arm.
source: Yet, the structures of different myosins vary, particularly in the orientation of the lever arm (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with other structures.

claim: The actomyosin interface of the rigor state of myosin-V is basically indistinguishable from the one in the strong-ADP state.
source: While the actomyosin interface of the rigor state of myosin-V is basically indistinguishable from the one in the strong-ADP state, the lever arm orientations of the two states differ by ~9° (Figure 3A, Figure 3—video 1A), in agreement with a previously reported rotation of 9.5° (Wulf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The lever arm orientations of the rigor and strong-ADP states differ by ~9°.
source: While the actomyosin interface of the rigor state of myosin-V is basically indistinguishable from the one in the strong-ADP state, the lever arm orientations of the two states differ by ~9° (Figure 3A, Figure 3—video 1A), in agreement with a previously reported rotation of 9.5° (Wulf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison and citations to established literature.

claim: The overall architecture of the rigor state structure is in good agreement with the medium-resolution cryo-EM structure published earlier.
source: The overall architecture of our rigor state structure not only is in good agreement with the medium-resolution cryo-EM structure published earlier (Wulf et al., 2016), but also strongly resembles the rigor-like crystal structures solved for this myosin isoform (Figure 2C–F; Coureux et al., 2003; Coureux et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with citations to established literature.

claim: The overall architecture of the rigor state structure strongly resembles the rigor-like crystal structures solved for myosin-V.
source: The overall architecture of our rigor state structure not only is in good agreement with the medium-resolution cryo-EM structure published earlier (Wulf et al., 2016), but also strongly resembles the rigor-like crystal structures solved for this myosin isoform (Figure 2C–F; Coureux et al., 2003; Coureux et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with citations to established literature.

claim: A comparison of the strong-ADP and rigor state structures allows the detailed description of the structural transition of myosin-V upon Mg2+-ADP release.
source: As the strong-ADP and rigor state represent sequential states within the myosin motor cycle, a comparison of the respective high-resolution structures allows the detailed description of the structural transition of myosin-V upon Mg2+-ADP release (Figure 3, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: The two sequential states (strong-ADP and rigor) differ primarily in their conformation of the central transducer β-sheet and the N-terminal domain, which twist and rotate, respectively.
source: In addition to the ~9° lever arm rotation described above (Figure 3A), the two sequential states differ primarily in their conformation of the central transducer β-sheet and the N-terminal domain, which twist and rotate, respectively (Figure 3C–E, Figure 3—video 1; see Figure 1—figure supplement 6 for an overview of the myosin domain architecture).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The structural changes upon Mg2+-ADP release are not transmitted to the U50 and L50 domains and thus do not alter the actin-binding interface.
source: Notably, the structural changes are not transmitted to the U50 and L50 domains and thus do not alter the actin-binding interface (Figure 3A and C, Figure 3—video 1A and B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The transducer rearrangements are directly linked to a reorganization of the active site that accounts for the reduced Mg2+-ADP affinity of the rigor state.
source: The transducer rearrangements are directly linked to a reorganization of the active site that accounts for the reduced Mg2+-ADP affinity of the rigor state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: Twisting of the transducer promotes a piston movement of the HF helix, increasing the distance between the P-loop and switch I, thereby opening the active site.
source: By promoting a piston movement of the HF helix, twisting of the transducer increases the distance between the P-loop and switch I, thereby opening the active site (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—video 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The resulting conformation after transducer twisting is incompatible with the Mg2+-coordinating hydrogen bond between the HF helix and switch II (T170-D437).
source: The resulting conformation is incompatible with the Mg2+-coordinating hydrogen bond between the HF helix and switch II (T170-D437).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: Loss of Mg2+ is thought to lead to the weak-ADP state of myosin.
source: Loss of Mg2+ is thought to lead to the weak-ADP state of myosin (Coureux et al., 2004), which is so named due to its low nucleotide affinity that promotes the release of ADP.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The weak-ADP state is so named due to its low nucleotide affinity that promotes the release of ADP.
source: Loss of Mg2+ is thought to lead to the weak-ADP state of myosin (Coureux et al., 2004), which is so named due to its low nucleotide affinity that promotes the release of ADP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the weak-ADP state.

claim: The subsequent rigor state is stabilized by a new network of hydrogen bonds formed between lysine K169 (HF helix) and aspartate D437 and isoleucine I438 (switch II).
source: The subsequent rigor state is stabilized by a new network of hydrogen bonds formed between lysine K169 (HF helix, previously coordinated to the β-phosphate of ADP), and aspartate D437 and isoleucine I438 (switch II).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: Upon Mg2+-ADP release, the A-loop undergoes a small lateral shift.
source: Upon Mg2+-ADP release, the A-loop also undergoes a small lateral shift (Figure 3B, D and E, Figure 3—video 1C and D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The A-loop likely stabilizes the twisting of the transducer and the N-terminal domain rotation.
source: In this way, it likely stabilizes the twisting of the transducer and the N-terminal domain rotation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: The role of the A-loop in both the coordination of ADP and the coupling of the active site to the periphery has not been fully appreciated previously.
source: Surprisingly, the role of the A-loop in both the coordination of ADP and the coupling of the active site to the periphery has not been fully appreciated previously, although it is also involved in nucleotide binding in other myosins (Bloemink et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference about the state of the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The A-loop is also involved in nucleotide binding in other myosins.
source: Surprisingly, the role of the A-loop in both the coordination of ADP and the coupling of the active site to the periphery has not been fully appreciated previously, although it is also involved in nucleotide binding in other myosins (Bloemink et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The P-loop, the A-loop, and switch I contribute to the sensing of the nucleotide state and its transmission from the nucleotide-binding pocket to the periphery.
source: Given their central importance for the coordination of Mg2+-ADP (Figure 1), we propose that the P-loop, the A-loop, and switch I contribute to the sensing of the nucleotide state and its transmission from the nucleotide-binding pocket to the periphery.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the structural data.

claim: The mutual interplay of the P-loop, A-loop, and switch I defines the orientation of the N-terminal domain relative to the U50 and L50 subdomains.
source: Their mutual interplay defines the orientation of the N-terminal domain relative to the U50 and L50 subdomains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Small changes in the active site (~1–2 Å) are amplified into significant rotations of the N-terminal and converter domain, eventually leading to a lever arm swing of ~9° upon Mg2+-ADP release.
source: In this way, small changes in the active site (~1–2 Å) are amplified into significant rotations of the N-terminal and converter domain, eventually leading to a lever arm swing of ~9° upon Mg2+-ADP release (Figure 3, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The high-resolution structures of the strong-ADP and rigor state are consistent with the sequential release of Mg2+ and ADP due to the isomerization of myosin to a conformation with reduced nucleotide affinity.
source: Our high-resolution structures of the strong-ADP and rigor state are consistent with the sequential release of Mg2+ and ADP due to the isomerization of myosin to a conformation with reduced nucleotide affinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: ADP binding to the rigor state can favor the reversal of the isomerization in the presence of Mg2+.
source: In line with this, ADP binding to the rigor state can favor the reversal of this isomerization in the presence of Mg2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: A similar structural transition upon Mg2+-ADP release has been reported for myosin-IB, -V, and -VI based on medium- and high-resolution cryo-EM structures.
source: A similar structural transition upon Mg2+-ADP release has been reported for myosin-IB, -V, and -VI based on medium- and high-resolution cryo-EM structures (Gurel et al., 2017; Mentes et al., 2018; Wulf et al., 2016), suggesting a common coupling mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The similar structural transition upon Mg2+-ADP release in myosin-IB, -V, and -VI suggests a common coupling mechanism.
source: A similar structural transition upon Mg2+-ADP release has been reported for myosin-IB, -V, and -VI based on medium- and high-resolution cryo-EM structures (Gurel et al., 2017; Mentes et al., 2018; Wulf et al., 2016), suggesting a common coupling mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with other structures.

claim: Most of the details of the structural transition upon Mg2+-ADP release are intriguingly similar across myosins, for example, the remodeling of hydrogen bonds due to the piston movement of the HF helix.
source: Although most of the details are intriguingly similar, for example, the remodeling of hydrogen bonds due to the piston movement of the HF helix (Mentes et al., 2018), we find notable differences in the extent of the lever arm swing associated with Mg2+-ADP release (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), as well as the conformation of the relay helix, which partially unwinds in myosin-IB and -VI to allow for the larger lever arm swings (Gurel et al., 2017; Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with citations to established literature.

claim: There are notable differences in the extent of the lever arm swing associated with Mg2+-ADP release across myosins.
source: Although most of the details are intriguingly similar, for example, the remodeling of hydrogen bonds due to the piston movement of the HF helix (Mentes et al., 2018), we find notable differences in the extent of the lever arm swing associated with Mg2+-ADP release (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), as well as the conformation of the relay helix, which partially unwinds in myosin-IB and -VI to allow for the larger lever arm swings (Gurel et al., 2017; Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with other structures.

claim: The relay helix partially unwinds in myosin-IB and -VI to allow for the larger lever arm swings.
source: Although most of the details are intriguingly similar, for example, the remodeling of hydrogen bonds due to the piston movement of the HF helix (Mentes et al., 2018), we find notable differences in the extent of the lever arm swing associated with Mg2+-ADP release (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), as well as the conformation of the relay helix, which partially unwinds in myosin-IB and -VI to allow for the larger lever arm swings (Gurel et al., 2017; Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Myosin-IB performs a larger lever arm swing (25°) upon Mg2+-ADP release compared to myosin-V (9° swing).
source: Interestingly, myosin-IB not only performs a larger lever arm swing (25°) (Mentes et al., 2018), but is also almost 40 times more sensitive to force than myosin-V (9° swing) (Laakso et al., 2008; Veigel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Myosin-IB is almost 40 times more sensitive to force than myosin-V.
source: Interestingly, myosin-IB not only performs a larger lever arm swing (25°) (Mentes et al., 2018), but is also almost 40 times more sensitive to force than myosin-V (9° swing) (Laakso et al., 2008; Veigel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The force sensitivity increases with the extent of the lever arm swing upon Mg2+-ADP release.
source: Since load will more easily prevent the isomerization of myosin if Mg2+-ADP release requires a large converter swing, we propose that the force sensitivity, which tunes the kinetics of the transition to the rigor state (Kovács et al., 2007; Laakso et al., 2008; Takagi et al., 2006; Veigel et al., 2005), increases with the extent of the lever arm swing upon Mg2+-ADP release.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the structural data and citations to established literature.

claim: The structure of F-actin-myosin-V in complex with AppNHp was determined with the aim to characterize a potentially short-lived, weakly bound state of myosin.
source: We determined the structure of F-actin-myosin-V in complex with the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AppNHp with the aim to characterize a potentially short-lived, weakly bound state of myosin.
evidence: This describes the experimental aim.

claim: The cryo-EM density map shows strong density for AppNHp, indicating high to complete saturation.
source: The resulting cryo-EM density map shows strong density for AppNHp, indicating high to complete saturation (Figure 4, Figure 4—video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The density suggests the presence of two ions, both likely corresponding to Mg2+.
source: Interestingly, the density also suggests the presence of two ions, both likely corresponding to Mg2+, given the size of the density and the buffer composition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM density maps and experimental conditions.

claim: One Mg2+ ion occupies approximately the position that Mg2+ takes in the active site of the strong-ADP state, namely close to the γ-phosphate of AppNHp.
source: While one ion occupies approximately the position that Mg2+ takes in the active site of the strong-ADP state, namely close to the γ-phosphate of AppNHp, the other one resides in between the α- and β-phosphates of AppNHp (Figures 1 and 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The other Mg2+ ion resides in between the α- and β-phosphates of AppNHp.
source: While one ion occupies approximately the position that Mg2+ takes in the active site of the strong-ADP state, namely close to the γ-phosphate of AppNHp, the other one resides in between the α- and β-phosphates of AppNHp (Figures 1 and 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: AppNHp is coordinated by a network of hydrogen bonds and additional hydrophobic interactions with the P-loop, switch I, and the A-loop, similar to ADP.
source: Similar to ADP, AppNHp is coordinated by a network of hydrogen bonds and additional hydrophobic interactions with the P-loop, switch I, and the A-loop (Figure 1C and Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: The details of the interactions differ between AppNHp and ADP due to the different sizes of the two nucleotides and their relative positions in the active site.
source: The details of the interactions, however, differ due to the different sizes of the two nucleotides and their relative positions in the active site, that is, the γ-phosphate of AppNHp almost takes the position of the β-phosphate of ADP relative to the HF helix (Figure 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The γ-phosphate of AppNHp almost takes the position of the β-phosphate of ADP relative to the HF helix.
source: The details of the interactions, however, differ due to the different sizes of the two nucleotides and their relative positions in the active site, that is, the γ-phosphate of AppNHp almost takes the position of the β-phosphate of ADP relative to the HF helix (Figure 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The overall structure of AppNHp-bound myosin-V is reminiscent of the rigor state, in contrast to a previous low-resolution cryo-EM reconstruction.
source: Surprisingly, and in contrast to a previous low-resolution cryo-EM reconstruction (Volkmann et al., 2005), the overall structure of AppNHp-bound myosin-V is reminiscent of the rigor state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison and contrasts with a citation to established literature.

claim: AppNHp-bound myosin is strongly bound to F-actin and adopts a post-powerstroke lever arm orientation.
source: In particular, myosin is strongly bound to F-actin and adopts a post-powerstroke lever arm orientation (Figure 4, Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: The active site of AppNHp-bound myosin closely resembles that of the rigor state, and thereby significantly deviates from the conformation found in the strong-ADP state.
source: The active site of AppNHp-bound myosin also closely resembles that of the rigor state, and thereby significantly deviates from the conformation found in the strong-ADP state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: The compatibility of an ATP analog with strong F-actin binding is initially puzzling and seemingly at odds with the reported reciprocal nature of these two processes.
source: The compatibility of an ATP analog, specifically the presence of a γ-phosphate at the active site, with strong F-actin binding is initially puzzling and seemingly at odds with the reported reciprocal nature of these two processes (Coureux et al., 2004; Kühner and Fischer, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and citations to established literature.

claim: A comparison of the AppNHp-bound structure with a rigor-like crystal structure of myosin-V with ADP weakly bound resolves the conflict of ATP analog compatibility with strong F-actin binding.
source: A comparison of our AppNHp-bound structure with a rigor-like crystal structure of myosin-V with ADP weakly bound to its active site (Coureux et al., 2004) resolves this conflict (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison and citations to established literature.

claim: The relative position of AppNHp and ADP in the AppNHp-bound and rigor-like structures as well as their coordination is almost identical.
source: The relative position of AppNHp and ADP in these two structures as well as their coordination, which in particular lacks contacts between K169 of the P-loop and the β-phosphate, is almost identical, suggesting that AppNHp is only weakly bound in our structure and therefore compatible with strong F-actin binding.
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural comparison.

claim: AppNHp is only weakly bound in the structure and therefore compatible with strong F-actin binding.
source: The relative position of AppNHp and ADP in these two structures as well as their coordination, which in particular lacks contacts between K169 of the P-loop and the β-phosphate, is almost identical, suggesting that AppNHp is only weakly bound in our structure and therefore compatible with strong F-actin binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: A similar coordination was observed for Mg2+-ADP in a putative strong-ADP to rigor transition state cryo-EM structure of myosin-IB.
source: Interestingly, a similar coordination was observed for Mg2+-ADP in a putative strong-ADP to rigor transition state cryo-EM structure of myosin-IB (Mentes et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The comparisons indicate that AppNHp and ADP can both weakly bind to myosin in a conformation reminiscent of the rigor.
source: These comparisons indicate that AppNHp and ADP can both weakly bind to myosin in a conformation reminiscent of the rigor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparisons.

source: Our prior kinetic studies (De La Cruz et al., 1999; Yengo et al., 2002) demonstrated that AppNHp reduces the binding affinity of myosin-V for F-actin by >5000-fold as compared to the rigor state, thus favoring dissociation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: AppNHp favors dissociation of myosin-V from F-actin.
source: Our prior kinetic studies (De La Cruz et al., 1999; Yengo et al., 2002) demonstrated that AppNHp reduces the binding affinity of myosin-V for F-actin by >5000-fold as compared to the rigor state, thus favoring dissociation.
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to established literature.

claim: A weakened affinity of AppNHp-bound myosin-V for F-actin is supported by the higher concentrations required to achieve decoration of F-actin with myosin in the AppNHp state.
source: A weakened affinity is also supported by the higher concentrations required to achieve decoration of F-actin with myosin in the AppNHp state (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental observations.

claim: AppNHp induces greater structural flexibility in myosin-V as compared to the rigor state.
source: AppNHp also induces greater structural flexibility in myosin-V (see below) as compared to the rigor state, which may facilitate the transition to a detached state.
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural analysis.

claim: Greater structural flexibility induced by AppNHp may facilitate the transition to a detached state.
source: AppNHp also induces greater structural flexibility in myosin-V (see below) as compared to the rigor state, which may facilitate the transition to a detached state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: The AppNHp-bound myosin-V structure represents a post-rigor transition (PRT) state that allows visualization of how ATP binds in the rigor state, prior to the transition that involves a switch I movement and promotes detachment of myosin from F-actin.
source: Based on the presented structural and prior kinetic studies, we propose that our AppNHp-bound myosin-V structure represents a post-rigor transtion (PRT) state that allows to visualize how ATP binds in the rigor state, prior to the transition that involves a switch I movement and promotes detachment of myosin from F-actin.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the structural data and citations to established literature.

claim: The characteristic weak coordination of AppNHp in the PRT state allows myosin to remain strongly bound to F-actin until a strong coordination of the nucleotide is established.
source: The characteristic weak coordination of AppNHp in the PRT state allows myosin to remain strongly bound to F-actin until a strong coordination of the nucleotide is established.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The report of a transition state with weakly bound ADP suggests that weak nucleotide binding is a common scheme.
source: The report of a transition state with weakly bound ADP (Mentes et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) suggests that weak nucleotide binding is a common scheme and that the PRT state is therefore not limited to AppNHp.
evidence: This is an inference based on a citation to established literature.

claim: The PRT state is not limited to AppNHp.
source: The report of a transition state with weakly bound ADP (Mentes et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) suggests that weak nucleotide binding is a common scheme and that the PRT state is therefore not limited to AppNHp.
evidence: This is an inference based on a citation to established literature.

claim: The visualization of an ATP analog bound to a state reminiscent of the rigor shows that ATP mainly binds via its adenine ring, as does ADP.
source: The visualization of an ATP analog bound to a state reminiscent of the rigor shows that ATP mainly binds via its adenine ring, as does ADP (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: The structure explains how the γ-phosphate can fit into the relatively small pocket created by the rigor conformation of the P-loop.
source: It also explains how the γ-phosphate can fit into the relatively small pocket created by the rigor conformation of the P-loop (Figure 4), and how its presence leads to local changes of the active site facilitating a tight coordination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The presence of the γ-phosphate leads to local changes of the active site facilitating a tight coordination.
source: It also explains how the γ-phosphate can fit into the relatively small pocket created by the rigor conformation of the P-loop (Figure 4), and how its presence leads to local changes of the active site facilitating a tight coordination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The PRT state provides new insights on how myosin detaches from F-actin.
source: In this way, the PRT state provides new insights on how myosin detaches from F-actin and indicates that the theoretical weakly bound post-rigor state (Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010; Walklate et al., 2016) is unlikely to be populated within the motor cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and citations to established literature.

claim: The theoretical weakly bound post-rigor state is unlikely to be populated within the motor cycle.
source: In this way, the PRT state provides new insights on how myosin detaches from F-actin and indicates that the theoretical weakly bound post-rigor state (Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010; Walklate et al., 2016) is unlikely to be populated within the motor cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and citations to established literature.

claim: Myosin-V-AppNHp is found strongly bound to F-actin in the PRT state.
source: Although we find myosin-V-AppNHp strongly bound to F-actin in the PRT state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we had to significantly increase the myosin concentration to achieve full decoration of actin filaments (see Materials and methods for details), in agreement with a weaker binding affinity (Konrad and Goody, 2005; Yengo et al., 2002).

claim: Significantly increased myosin concentration was required to achieve full decoration of actin filaments with AppNHp-bound myosin, in agreement with a weaker binding affinity.
source: Although we find myosin-V-AppNHp strongly bound to F-actin in the PRT state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we had to significantly increase the myosin concentration to achieve full decoration of actin filaments (see Materials and methods for details), in agreement with a weaker binding affinity (Konrad and Goody, 2005; Yengo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental observations and citations to established literature.

claim: AppNHp can potentially lead to different structural states, similar to ADP in myosin-IB.
source: We therefore conclude that AppNHp can potentially lead to different structural states, similar to ADP in myosin-IB (Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and citations to established literature.

source: Likely due to large differences in the binding affinity of these states or rapid detachment of myosin from F-actin, we only find myosin bound to F-actin in the PRT state.

claim: A comparison of the three states of the actomyosin-V complex (strong-ADP, rigor, and PRT state) reveals a striking similarity of the actomyosin interface.
source: A comparison of the three states of the actomyosin-V complex (strong-ADP, rigor, and PRT state) reveals a striking similarity of the actomyosin interface (Figure 5, Figure 5—video 1).

claim: The rearrangements, especially along the first PC, are reminiscent of the structural transition of myosin-V upon Mg2+-ADP release.

source: In line with this, we find the strong-ADP and rigor average structures to be arranged diagonally within the PC 1–PC 2 space (Figure 10A).

source: This indicates that the conformational heterogeneity of myosin-V as well as the isomerization associated with Mg2+-ADP release relies on the same principal coupling mechanism.

source: Furthermore, this suggests that the structural transition of myosin-V along its motor cycle is driven, at least in part, by its conformational flexibility.

source: Based on this, we therefore propose that the active site of myosin-V is not mechanically, and thus rigidly, coupled to the surrounding domains, particularly the lever arm, as previously proposed (Fischer et al., 2005).

source: Rather, its coupling seems to be statistical in nature, ultimately leading to a thermodynamic ensemble of conformations within each state.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the data analysis.

source: The associated structural flexibility of myosin-V possibly initiates transitions between structural states by giving rise to short-lived intermediate conformations with favorable nucleotide-binding affinities.

source: Interactions with a nucleotide would consequently not trigger the transition, but merely stabilize myosin in its transient conformation, thereby promoting the transition to a new structural ensemble state.

claim: A non-rigid, stochastic coupling of the active site of myosin-V is in good agreement with the release of Mg2+-ADP due to an isomerization as well as the existence of the PRT state.
source: A non-rigid, stochastic coupling of the active site of myosin-V is in good agreement with the release of Mg2+-ADP due to an isomerization as well as the existence of the PRT state.

source: It also provides a good explanation for the different binding affinities of the rigor and strong-ADP state.

source: Specifically, we propose that the extent of conformational heterogeneity tunes the binding affinity rather than changes in the actomyosin interface since these are almost the same in all three nucleotide states studied (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the data analysis.

claim: Restrictions of the conformational space by external forces, that is, load on the lever arm, could account for the load dependence of transitions within the cycle, such as the delay of ADP release under load.
source: Restrictions of the conformational space by external forces, that is, load on the lever arm, could account for the load dependence of transitions within the cycle, such as the delay of ADP release under load (Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data analysis and citations to established literature.

claim: The conformational flexibility observed as well as the conclusions on its role in the motor cycle are in line with more than two decades of molecular spectroscopy experiments, which have primarily, but not exclusively, studied myosin-II.
source: The conformational flexibility we observe (Figures 9 and 10) as well as our conclusions on its role in the motor cycle are in line with more than two decades of molecular spectroscopy experiments, which have primarily, but not exclusively, studied myosin-II.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with established literature.

claim: Site-directed labeling has demonstrated that myosin is highly dynamic and that multiple, functionally relevant structural states coexist within a single biochemical state.
source: In particular, site-directed labeling has demonstrated that myosin is highly dynamic and that multiple, functionally relevant structural states coexist within a single biochemical state (Forkey et al., 2003; Nesmelov et al., 2008; Nesmelov et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: It was shown that neither the active site is tightly coupled to the structural domains of the motor nor are the domains themselves.
source: Moreover, it was shown that neither the active site is tightly coupled to the structural domains of the motor nor are the domains themselves (Klein et al., 2008; Korman et al., 2006; Naber et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The results extend the spectroscopic data by directly visualizing the dynamics of myosin as well as the underlying molecular coupling.
source: Our results extend the spectroscopic data, which have already elucidated conformational amplitudes and kinetics, by directly visualizing the dynamics of myosin as well as the underlying molecular coupling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and comparison with established literature.

claim: The agreement of the results with the spectroscopic data on myosin-II suggests that statistical coupling and conformational flexibility are general features of the myosin superfamily, rather than a hallmark of myosin-V.
source: While the agreement of our results with the spectroscopic data on myosin-II (Thomas et al., 2009) already suggests that statistical coupling and conformational flexibility are general features of the myosin superfamily, rather than a hallmark of myosin-V, there are additional independent indications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with established literature.

source: On the one hand, statistical coupling of the active site has also been proposed for myosin-VI based on a recovery stroke intermediate crystal structure, showing that the lever arm can partially re-prime while the active site remains unchanged (Blanc et al., 2018).

source: On the other hand, conformational heterogeneity has also been reported for myosin-IE and -IB based on either crystal structures or cryo-EM data of the actomyosin complex (Behrmann et al., 2012; Kollmar et al., 2002; Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A flexibility reminiscent of the one observed for myosin-V was reported for myosin-IE in the rigor state.
source: Notably, a flexibility reminiscent of the one observed for myosin-V (Figures 9 and 10) was reported for myosin-IE in the rigor state (Behrmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

source: Conversely, no flexibility was described for myosin-IB, which adopts a single state in the absence of a nucleotide and two discrete states when bound to Mg2+-ADP (Mentes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

source: In general, there is little structural data on the conformational dynamics of myosin as most structures originate either from small cryo-EM data sets, which have an insufficient number of particles for extensive 3D classifications, or from X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

source: We therefore believe that the structural characterization of myosin's dynamic landscape will provide novel insights into the details of force generation.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of future research.
